sentences.text: By way of these applications under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the applicants have prayed to quash and set aside the FIR being C.R. No.38 of 2015 registered with Kalol Taluka Police Station, for the offences under Sections 406, 465, 467, 468 and 114 of the IPC.
2. It is the case of the petitioner that dispute pertains to various parcels of land situated at village Borisana, Taluka Kalol, District Gandhinagar.
The original landowners had executed two registered agreements for sale in favour of one Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel.
Thereafter, said Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel executed an agreement for sale in favour of the present applicant as well as in favour of one Amrishbhai Patel.

2.1. Subsequently, with the alleged intent to frustrate the rights of NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined the present applicant over the said Manoj Vinodchandra Shah vs State Of Gujarat on 7 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/74450037/
1 lands, Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel, in collusion with the complainant, executed two further agreements for sale on 21.04.2012 in favour of the complainant.

sentences.text: Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel also instituted Special Civil Suit No. 82 of 2013 against the present applicant and Amrishbhai Patel seeking cancellation of the earlier agreement for sale dated 20.02.2012, wherein no interim relief was granted in his favour.

Thereafter, the complainant lodged the impugned complaint being I-C.R.
No. 38 of 2015 before Kalol Taluka Police Station, leading to the filing of the present Special Criminal Application seeking quashment of the said complaint.

3. Heard learned advocate Mr. Tapan K. Patel for the petitioners, learned advocate Ms. Bhavana Acharya for the respondent No.2 (original complainant), and learned APP Mr. Chintan Dave for the respondent-State.
4.

Learned advocate for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner had entered into an agreement to sell with one Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel, whereby various parcels of land were agreed to be sold to the petitioner.

It is submitted that on 20.02.2012, Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel, claiming himself to be an agreement-holder in respect of the said parcels of land, executed the agreement to sell in favour of the petitioner.
Thereafter, on 21.04.2012, Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel is stated to have executed another agreement to sell in favour of the private respondent/complainant.
It is submitted NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined that now two agreement to sale holder are fighting with each other.

It is thus contended that the dispute is essentially a civil dispute between two agreement-holders seeking rights over the same land, and the allegations in the FIR do not disclose the commission of any criminal offence, much less the offences alleged.

It is further submitted that the ingredients of Section 406 of the IPC are conspicuously absent, and as such, the impugned FIR deserves to be quashed in exercise of the inherent jurisdiction of this Court.
4.1.
Like wise, no allegation are alleged that forged documents are prepared and used as genuine.
Thus, even ingredient of offence under Sections 465, 467 and 114 of the IPC are also failed to be attracted.
4.2. Upon above submission it is submitted to allow the petition and to quash impugned FIR.

5. Per contra, learned advocate appearing for respondent No.2 submitted that the complainant had agreed to purchase the subject land from Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel prior in point of time and had even paid earnest money towards the said transaction.

Despite being aware of this prior agreement,
Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel proceeded to execute another agreement to sell in favour of the present petitioner, thereby giving rise to the alleged offences under Sections 406, 465, 467, and 114 of the IPC.
It is contended that the conduct of the petitioner is not bonafide and prima facie constitutes criminal NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined culpability.
6. Learned APP for the respondent-State submitted that in light of the factual controversy and the nature of the dispute, this Court may pass appropriate orders in accordance with law.

sentences.text: Having heard the learned advocates for the respective parties and having perused the material placed on record, it prima facie appears that the land in question belongs to one Rochitji Chundaji Thakor and five other agriculturists.
As per the FIR, it was originally agreed by the agriculturists to sell the land to Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel, and two separate agreements to sell were executed.
However, Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel, despite having paid part of the sale consideration, failed to pay the balance amount and could not get the sale deed executed in his favour.

Thereafter, he proceeded to execute two separate agreements to sell without consent of agriculturists who are owner of parcel of land--one in favour of the present petitioner on 20.02.2012, and another in favour of the complainant on 21.04.2012.
As per the version of the complainant, the agreement to sell was preceded by negotiations and a token payment made on 10.02.2012.
8. In the backdrop of the aforesaid chequered factual history, what emerges is a civil dispute between two competing agreement- holders.
Both agreements to sell are unregistered and executed without the title of the seller being perfected.

No sale deed has been NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined executed by the original agriculturist owners in favour of Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel or other party competing with each other through FIR.
9.

In Meghmala & Ors. v. G. Narasimha Reddy & Ors. [(2010) 8 SCC 383], the Hon'ble Supreme Court categorically held that an agreement to sell, by itself, does not create any right, title, or interest in favour of the prospective purchaser.

Similarly, in Suraj Lamp and Industries Pvt. Ltd. v.
State of Haryana & Anr. [(2011) SCALE 438], it was held that the transfer of immovable property by way of sale can be effected only by a registered instrument of conveyance, and in the absence thereof, no right, title, or interest passes in law.

sentences.text: 10. The FIR reveals that Hardik Vasudevbhai Patel executed agreements in favour of both the petitioner and the complainant, allegedly without the knowledge or consent of the original agriculturist landowners.
The dispute, therefore, stems from conflicting claims arising out of unregistered agreements to sell, which, in the considered view of this Court, lacks the essential ingredients of criminality.
It appears that an essentially civil dispute has been given a colour of criminal proceedings, which is impermissible in law.

11. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Radheshyam v. State of Rajasthan, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2311, it has been held NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined as under:-

sentences.text: As already indicated above, a perusal of the complaint which has been registered as the FIR does not spell out any element or ingredient of cheating or breach of trust.
Mere non-performance of an Agreement to Sell by itself does not amount to cheating and breach of trust.
Respondent no. 2 has adequate remedy of filing a Civil Suit for relief of specific performance of a contract which he has already availed and the suit is still pending.
The FIR only appears to be an arm- twisting mechanism to pressurise the appellants to execute the Sale Deed or to extract money.
Every civil wrong cannot be converted into a criminal wrong.

As we find in the present case, respondent no. 2 Manoj Vinodchandra Shah vs State Of Gujarat on 7 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/74450037/
3 is trying to abuse the criminal machinery for ulterior motives.

sentences.text: It is not his case that the appellants duped him to pay the advance amount and entered into an Agreement to Sell.
The High Court fell in error in recording a finding that the ingredients of offences under sections 420 and 406 of IPC are present in the instant case.

7. Section 420, IPC provides that:
"Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine."
For an offence under Section 420, IPC, the following ingredients must be present:
i. Cheating as defined under Section 415, IPC, that is, there should be a fraudulent or dishonest inducement of a person; ii. An intention to deceive; and iii.

The person cheated must be dishonestly induced to a. Deliver property to any person; or b. Make,
alter or destroy valuable security or anything signed or sealed and capable of being converted into valuable security.
NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined 8.
Thus, cheating forms an essential ingredient to constitute and offence under Section 420, IPC.

Further, to constitute cheating as defined under Section 415, IPC, it is necessary that a fraudulent or dishonest inducement is done and the deceived person is made to deliver any property owing to the fraud.

Section 415, IPC,
defines'cheating', as:
"Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind,
reputation or property,

is said to "cheat"."
9.
From the bare perusal of the FIR, it is evident that there was no act of cheating, that is, the complainant was nowhere fraudulently induced or dishonestly deceived by the appellants.
A commercial transaction took place between the parties during which the parties consensually agreed for the sale of the property of the appellants and respondent no. 2 paid the part consideration.
The default in payment of their loan dues on part of the appellants is not reflective of their deceitful intention towards the complainant.
Mere non- registration of the sale or its refusal cannot amount to cheating.

It is a civil dispute and gives rise to the complainant's right to resort to the remedies provided under civil law by filing a suit for specific performance.
10. Additionally, the appellants have also been accused of committing the offence of criminal breach of trust under Section 406, IPC.

This offence is defined under Section 405, IPC as follows:
NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED: 07/08/2025 undefined "Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes off that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract,
express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits "criminal breach of trust"."

The accused had dishonestly misappropriated or converted to their own use that property, or dishonestly used or disposed of that property or wilfully suffer any other person to do so; and iii. Such misappropriation, conversion, use or disposal should be in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract which the person has made, touching the discharge of such trust.
12. In the present case, the appellants were not entrusted with any property by respondent no. 2 - complainant.
The only delivery made was of part payment towards an Agreement to Sell between the parties.
The amount paid towards consideration cannot be said to have been entrusted with the appellants by respondent no. 2.
Additionally, merely because the appellants are refusing to register the sale, it does not amount to misappropriation of the advance payment.
Since there was no entrustment of property, the offence of misappropriation of such property and thereby criminal breach of trust cannot be said to be made out."

12. Applying the dictum laid down in Radheshyam (supra) to the facts at hand, it is evident that dispute is fundamentally civil in NEUTRAL CITATION R/SCR.A/1849/2015 ORDER DATED:
07/08/2025 undefined nature and the remedy, if any, lies before the competent civil forum.

It is trite to state that the jurisdiction of this Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. can be invoked to prevent abuse of the process of law and to secure the ends of justice, particularly where continuation of prosecution would amount to sheer harassment and serve no fruitful purpose.
